sections.summary: The Government is being given the power to issue Restraining Orders relating to race.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Government is being given the power to issue Restraining Orders relating to race.

sections.label: Affirmative answer
sections.summary: The reply states that as a matter of fact, that is yes.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As a matter of fact, that is yes.

sections.label: President acts on Cabinet advice
sections.summary: Under FICA, the President cannot independently veto the Cabinet or Minister and must act on Cabinet advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: In that case, under FICA, the President does not have the power to independently veto the decision of the Cabinet or the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He has got to act on the advice of the Cabinet.

sections.label: Minister versus Court decisions
sections.summary: Under current law the Court decides whether something is criminal, but clause 8 gives that decision to the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: The main difference is that under current law, decisions are made by the Court on whether it is criminal, but in clause 8, the decision is made by the Minister.

sections.label: Phrases, umbrellas and offences
sections.summary: The speaker asked whether certain phrases and watermelon-painted umbrellas would draw a Restraining Order or clause 40 prosecution, and said prior offences remain offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Would individuals who use such phrases, such as "from river to sea, Palestinians will be free" online or offline, now we subject to a Restraining Order under this Bill or be prosecuted under clause 40 of the Bill?" Then, she asked about those who use umbrellas painted with watermelon: "Would individuals committing such acts be subject to a Restraining Order or prosecuted under clause 40 of the Bill?" And my point generally was that, if it was an offence previously, it is an offence now.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If it was not an offence previously, it would not be an offence now.

sections.label: Restraining Order under clause 8
sections.summary: Clause 8's Restraining Order essentials resemble sections 298 and 298A, except the decision is made by the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There are four other aspects, one of which is the Restraining Order under clause 8.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But if you look at the provisions of clause 8, the essentials that need to be satisfied, they are similar to the requirements of sections 298, 298A, except that the decision is made by the Minister.

sections.label: President's veto power question
sections.summary: The question asks why the Minister gives the President veto power under the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act but not under FICA.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And ultimately, I have talked about the routes for challenging the Minister's decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: So, why does the Minister see fit to give the President the veto power under the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act, but not under FICA?

sections.label: Intelligence tracking and disclosure
sections.summary: Such information is usually tracked through own or exchanged intelligence, and disclosing it beyond a small group of intelligence officers would seriously prejudice national interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And usually, it is tracked through intelligence, either intelligence by ourselves or sometimes through intelligence exchange with others too.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It would be a serious prejudice to national interest if we were to go out and disclose to anyone beyond a very small group of intelligence officers the nature of this information.

sections.label: Good faith defence on balance
sections.summary: A defence is being put in where the person need not prove beyond reasonable doubt but on a balance of probabilities that he acted in good faith and tried to remove what he did or said.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Unlike some other situations, here, we are actually trying to put in a defence that if the person can show and he is not required to prove it beyond reasonable doubt, but on a balance of probabilities, that his conduct, even though the conduct would be causing these effects, he acted in good faith and he actually tried to remove whatever he had done or said.

sections.label: Relevance of intention to offence
sections.summary: The intention is relevant first of all to whether an offence has in fact been committed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The intention is relevant to, first of all, whether an offence has, in fact, been committed.

sections.label: Intention behind section 40(6)
sections.summary: The intention behind section 40(6) was to add defences for people who made comments in a certain context but in good faith try to undo the damage.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Without knowing in detail what the artist has done, I am loathe to go further.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But the intention behind section 40(6) was actually to try and add in additional defences to support people who might have made comments in a certain context, but then, in good faith, try and undo the damage.
